cim: Így kerülhető el az AI-modellek utasításvesztése a beszélgetésekben
lead: A kutatások szerint a többüzenetes párbeszédekben 39 százalékkal romlik a modellek pontossága, de jobb promptolás helyett más trükkök segítenek.
osszefoglalo:
A Microsoft és a Salesforce közös kutatása szerint a nyelvi modellek teljesítménye átlagosan **39 százalékkal romlik**, ha egy feladatot nem egyben, hanem több üzenetre bontva kapnak meg. Ennek fő oka a kontextus közepén lévő információk elvesztése, így a beszélgetés közben küldött javítások vagy emlékeztetők a legkevésbé hatékonyak.

A probléma megelőzésére a leghatékonyabb módszer a szabályok projektszintű utasításokba foglalása, mivel ezek minden üzenetnél érvényesülnek. Ha egy válasz mégis rosszul sikerül, a mid-chat javító üzenet helyett a korábbi **üzenet szerkesztése** a megoldás, ami új ágat nyit a beszélgetésben, és kitorli a hibás választ a kontextusból.

Amennyiben a modell másodszor is eltér az utasításoktól, érdemes összefoglalót kérni az addigiakról, majd **új beszélgetést indítani**. Egy friss chatben az összes információt egyetlen promptba sűrítve a modell a legjobb teljesítményének közel 95 százalékát nyújtja, miközben az elhasznált kontextusablak és a költségek is csökkennek.
miert_szamit: Beszélgetés közbeni javítgatás helyett az **üzenetek szerkesztésével vagy új chat indításával** sokkal pontosabb válaszokat kapsz és kevesebb tokent fogyasztasz.

cim_eredeti: Claude has a drift problem, and the fix wasn't better prompting
szoveg_eredeti:
Anyone who's used Claude has probably encountered its drift problem from time to time. You set a rule in the first message, even something simple like how a reply should be formatted, it holds up for about a dozen turns then starts slipping. Further in, Claude seems to start answering a different question than the one you asked, or suddenly agrees with something it pushed back on earlier.

Although drift is expected to happen when you run out of context, that's not what I'm talking about here. Claude drift can happen earlier in a session or in short sessions too. Drift is what users report as Claude gradually veering off the instructions you gave it, even though the session is nowhere near running out of room. I found a way to reel it back in, and it has nothing to do with writing better prompts.

Drift simply means the chat drifts away from your instructions, specific nuggets of information you told it to keep in mind, or the theme of the session as a whole. Anthropic reports scores on a test that gets close to this issue, called MRCR v2, which hides eight near-identical requests across a million tokens of conversation and asks the model to repeat back its answer to one specific request. When Opus 4.6 launched in February, it scored 76% on that version of the test, while Sonnet 4.5 managed 18.5% on the same one.

I use the Opus models for most of my tasks and it still happens to me though. I reckon a stronger model helps a bit, but honestly I can't say how much since MRCR checks whether Claude can find something buried in a chat and not whether it keeps doing what you asked. A Microsoft and Salesforce study that simulated over 200,000 conversations across 15 models, Claude 3.7 Sonnet among them, found the models performed about 39% worse on average when a task was spread over several messages instead of given all at once. The drop was about the same size for strong models as for weaker ones.

The Lost in the Middle paper found models use information best when it's at the start or end of what they're reading, and worst when it's somewhere in the middle. I reckon that's bad news for the reminders and corrections you send halfway through a session, since every one of them lands somewhere in that middle.

For me, one of the most annoying Claude drift problems is the em dash. I used to love the em dash and used it constantly before AI became a thing. But now it's so heavily associated with robotic AI responses, it's become really annoying to see in any response; it almost feels like the model is mocking me when it responds with em dashes. So I'm constantly finding myself telling Claude to not respond with em dashes because it seems to constantly lose that instruction somewhere in the middle of a session. But I've found a couple more effective ways of getting Claude to stick to my rules and stay on topic.

Project instructions are the closest thing Claude chat has to the CLAUDE.md file people use in Claude Code. Whatever you write there applies to every conversation in that project, and these rules tend to hold much more reliably throughout a session than rules you add to the first message. If you'd rather skip projects, you could upload a rules document to an individual session, but you might find yourself having to remind Claude about the doc or uploading it again halfway through.

The reason projects are more effective than rules you type mid-chat comes back to that middle of the chat. A rule that gets typed into the conversation gets pushed back further and further as the chat grows, while project instructions are already in place when the chat starts and gets taken into account with every response. If you upload files to a project instead, keep in mind that once they get close, Claude switches to RAG and searches them only for the relevant bits instead of absorbing the full thing.
